newsitem.title: USA: Fed mulls next role in U.S. payments system.
newsitem.headline: Fed mulls next role in U.S. payments system.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is mulling its future role in the U.S. payments system under five scenarios that go from downsizing its huge operations to spearheading high-tech innovations, Fed sources said.

The outcome of the debate -- either way -- may profoundly change the world's largest payments system that handles about 45 billion checks and 3 billion small-value electronic transfers a year, they added.
It would also determine whether the U.S. central bank or the private sector will take the leadership in that sector.
"These are not actual proposals but scenarios for discussion with stakeholders, meaning those who have a stake in the functions the Fed performs," a Fed source told Reuters.
"The scenarios are to generate a discussion. We welcome input from the stakeholders as well," the source added.
The five scenarios are spelled out in a Fed document, "Alternatives Roles for the Federal Reserve in the Interbank Retail Payment Systems," of which Reuters obtained a copy.
They were drafted by the committee headed by Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin to consider how technology and the new Interstate Banking Act may affect the payments system.
Under the five different scenarios, the Fed would either:
-- entirely withdraw from check collection and Automated Clearinghouse (ACH) services that process small payments,
-- privatize its check collection and ACH operations by setting up a clearing bank with no tie to the Fed,
-- continue to provide check collection and ACH services, but only if under-recovery of costs is allowed,
-- promote efficiency among commercial providers and operate in specific areas only if under-recovery is allowed,
-- speed up the move to an electronic-based retail payment system if under-recovery of costs is allowed where needed.
The Monetary Control Act currently bars the Fed from operating below costs although these vary across regions.
"The question is what kind of payments system services should the Fed provide in the 21st century, and at what price," another Fed source told Reuters.
"If the Fed is to perform a public service, the issue of cost recovery must be addressed," the source added.

The central bank handled about 15 billion checks and about 2.5 billion ACH transactions in 1996, requiring a large staff and complex operations to provide interbank services to about 23,000 depository institutions and the Treasury.

"The sense is that the private sector would want to go after the segments of the business that promise the best commercial rewards but would not necessarily want to provide services everywhere, as the Fed does," the Fed source added.
The source predicted private competitors would be ready to pick up the Fed's business in densily populated areas where volume amortizes costs -- but unwilling to operate everywhere.

Some specialists at the Fed want the Fed to remain the leader in the payments system and seek innovations setting the benchmark for the private sector, which may "generate more profits for the Fed," the source added.
The Rivlin committee's report said "This strategy would include Federal Reserve funding for research and development, ... direct investment to foster efficiency."
Though the Fed looks favorably upon all-electronic payments, the report acknowledged that a quick reduction in the volume of checks may ironically push the pricing of electronic services higher.
"A reduced check operation would absorb a smaller share of the Federal Reserve's fixed overhead costs such as buildings, personnel and security," the report said.

Regardless of the decision taken about check handling and ACH operations, there is no plan to tinker with Fedwire that handles much large single transactions, does not bundle transfers, and guarantees final settlement.
The Fed's keeping of electronic book entries or its role as fiscal agent for the Treasury, foreign central banks and international organizations are not in question either.
